newsitem.title: UK: EU sugar premiums stay low before new crop arrives.
newsitem.headline: EU sugar premiums stay low before new crop arrives.

text.p: Slack demand for white sugar from the European Union's new beet crop has kept quoted premiums at low levels for the rest of this year and producers see little incentive to move cargoes, physical brokers said on Thursday.
Premiums for new crop EU sugars were quoted at around $6 over London's spot December contract, based on ex-Antwerp shipment in October/November, and about $1 higher for December.
"In Europe it's right at the beginning and it's all fine -- the new crop is available from October 10 and there seems to be plenty," said one physical sugar broker.

Another trade source said current price differences between forward futures contracts gave little reason for producers to hurry to sell their cargoes, possibly preferring to wait until the London market turns upwards.
"You're probably looking to move August sugar at the same sort of level and on a flat price basis it makes no difference," the trader said.
"Producers really feel no pressure to move sugar out -- there's no advantage unless they have a cash flow problem."
Demand is also slack even though cargoes from the new crop will soon be available and relieve the tight supply situation. Little if no sugar is thought to remain from the 1995/96 crop.
"As much as there aren't many offers around, there isn't much demand around," said one market source.

The EU is widely expected to face increasing competition from Middle East refineries in satisfying local demand for quality whites, although there have been reports of traditional EU buyers taking lesser quality material due to lower prices.
"A lot of the European traditional markets for 45 ICUMSA white sugar used to be the Middle East and now you've got the Middle East refineries buying raws," the source said.
"It is envisaged that a lot of the Middle East buyers are not going to be taking the European sugar they used to in the past," he said.

The region's second sugar refinery in Jeddah should come on stream in early 1997 with an annual capacity of 500,000 tonnes. It is expected to take its first raws from Australia and then look at Brazil, Cuba, Thailand and South Africa as suppliers.
Refining began last year at the 720,000 tonne capacity Al Khaleej plant at Jebel Ali in Dubai.
Traders said the Saudi refinery could pose more of a threat to the EU as a quality whites supplier as it would probably be more efficient than Dubai, despite its lower capacity.
"It (Jeddah) is going to get much more into its stride than Dubai...and be much more professionally run," the trader said.
"The trade down there are not really buying much sugar at all," he said.
He added that many local traders who were importers bought sugar before London market prices fell and now had long futures positions which were some $10 above current world prices.
Oman is also reported as being interested in building a refinery in Muscat to produce 180,000 tonnes of sugar a year. The plant is expected to come on stream in early 1998.

But the Arabian peninsula, where annual sugar consumption is among the highest in the world at an average 30 kg per head, will remain a net importer of refined sugar despite the increased local production.
The UAE, Bahrain, Oman, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Yemen, which together consume about 1.6 million tonnes, will still be in deficit of about 200,000 tonnes.
